title: Packing records like C
description:
Write and read the bytes of a C structure with Python's `struct` module, so that a C program (or a file it wrote) and Python agree byte for byte. Use the layout rules of practice 6.02.

```python
def struct_format(fields, pack=None): ...
def pack_record(fields, values, pack=None): ...
def unpack_record(fields, data, pack=None): ...
```

`fields` uses the types of practice 6.02. Each type has a `struct` code:

| Type | Code | Python value |
|---|---|---|
| `char` | `c` | `bytes` of length 1 |
| `bool` | `?` | `bool` |
| `int8_t`, `uint8_t` | `b`, `B` | `int` |
| `short`, `int16_t`, `uint16_t` | `h`, `h`, `H` | `int` |
| `int`, `int32_t`, `uint32_t` | `i`, `i`, `I` | `int` |
| `float`, `double` | `f`, `d` | `float` |
| `long long`, `int64_t`, `uint64_t`, `pointer` | `q`, `q`, `Q`, `Q` | `int` |

**struct_format** returns the format: `<` (little-endian, no automatic padding), then for each field the padding before it as `Nx` (only when N > 0) followed by its code, then any padding at the end as `Nx`. An array `char[n]` is `ns` (one `bytes` value); any other array `T[n]` is `n` followed by T's code (a list of n values).

**pack_record** takes a dict of values by field name and returns the bytes (`struct` fills a short `char[n]` value with zero bytes). **unpack_record** returns the dict back; arrays (other than `char[n]`) come back as lists. Data whose length is not the structure's size raises `ValueError`.
hints: Compute the padding before each field and after the last one exactly as in practice 6.02, and write it into the format as `Nx`. With `<`, `struct` adds no padding of its own, so your `x` codes are the only padding.
`struct.pack` takes a flat list of values: a non-character array contributes one value per element, and `unpack` gives them back flat, so regroup them into lists.
